steps.title: A small header, then the SPL, and what the SPL does first
steps.body: Left: the 131,676 bytes of `BOOT.BIN` from this build. Right: the five tables of register writes that `ps7_init()` replays before anything else can run. The BootROM only needs the header to be right; the SPL needs the tables to be right.

steps.title: The header is what the BootROM checks
steps.body: 2,240 bytes (0x8C0) written by `mkimage -T zynqimage`. If any of the fields below is wrong, the ROM refuses the file and the board stays silent: there is no UART yet to complain on.

steps.title: Identifier, width detection and where the payload starts
steps.body:
`0xAA995566` at 0x20 lets the ROM detect the bus width of the boot device and `XNLX` at 0x24 says this is a Zynq boot image. The image offset, `0x8C0`, says the SPL begins right after the header.

A Xilinx-built `BOOT.BIN` with an FSBL, a bitstream and U-Boot has a partition table in this area; this one has a single partition.

steps.title: Size, load address and checksum
steps.body: `mkimage` records the file's size (131,676 bytes) and a load address of 0: the ROM copies the SPL to the start of the on-chip RAM, and the SPL is linked to run there. The checksum field (0xFD164EC9 here) is the complement of the sum of the fields above it.

steps.title: The payload is the SPL, 129,436 bytes
steps.body: ARM code plus the SPL's own device tree. It contains the compiled register tables, the UART and SD drivers, a FAT reader and a FIT parser. It must stay below 192 KiB: `uboot.sh` fails the build if `boot.bin` is bigger.

steps.title: ps7_init, step 1: the pin muxes
steps.body: The Zynq has 54 multiplexed I/O pins. This table connects each to a peripheral: UART0 on 14/15, the SD host on 40-45, Ethernet on 16-27, USB on 28-39, QSPI on 1-6. The mapping is the board designer's, written down in the hardware design.

steps.title: Steps 2 and 3: PLLs, then clock dividers
steps.body: The 33.3333 MHz oscillator feeds three PLLs (ARM, DDR, IO). The clock table then divides them for the CPUs, the DDR controller and each peripheral. A wrong divider here is why a console prints garbage.

steps.title: Step 4: the DDR3L comes alive
steps.body: The DDR table programs the controller for DDR3, a 32-bit data bus and 1 GiB, and polls the calibration status. Everything after this line, including U-Boot proper and the kernel, lives in this memory.

steps.title: Step 5: the last registers, then relock
steps.body: UART and QSPI controller registers, SMC timing and the PL power-on-reset registers, ending by locking the SLCR (the system-level control registers) again. After `ps7_init` returns, the SPL prints its banner on UART0.

steps.anchor: Why this is a table of register writes
steps.title: Generated by Vivado, not written by hand
steps.body: Each array is a list of address/mask/value records that `ps7_config()` replays. The file carries three versions for silicon revisions 1.0, 2.0 and 3.0 and picks one at run time. It is a function of the board's hardware design, which is why it is an input of the build and not part of U-Boot.
